burton_span.exact: or of greater note, because oftentimes the passions of the stomach concur with them

source.author: Filotheo Montalto (Montaltus)

1.3.2.1-f5.text: Si nulla digna laesio ventriculo, quoniam in hac melancholia capitis, exigua nonnunquam ventriculi pathemata coeunt, duo enim haec membra sibi invicem affectionem transmittunt

translations.literal: If no worthy injury to the stomach, since in this melancholy of the head small sometimes of-the-stomach passions come together, for these two members to one another the affection transmit
translations.note: 'digna' (worthy, i.e. notable) is the word Burton picks up in his text. The stomach and the brain passing an affection to each other is the old medical idea of sympathy, or 'consent', between organs. Burton's own English renders only the first part of the note.

translations.text: If there is no notable injury to the stomach; for in this melancholy of the head slight affections of the stomach sometimes concur, since these two members pass the affection to each other.

translations.note: The sentence opens with a conditional 'si' and is not completed in the quotation. Burton's English at the anchor renders only the 'digna' and 'concur' portion loosely. Montaltus is named in the main text at the anchor.

translations.text: If there is no notable lesion of the stomach—since in this melancholy of the head some slight disorders of the stomach sometimes concur, for these two parts transmit affection to each other in turn
